takeaways: An array pattern is the element pattern times an array factor that depends only on spacing, phase step and number of elements.
For two elements |AF| = 2|cos(ψ/2)| with ψ = βd cosθ + α; beams sit at ψ = 0 and nulls at ψ = ±π inside the visible range.
Broadside needs α = 0 and d < λ; end-fire needs α = −βd and d < λ/2. End-fire is wider in angle but twice as directive for the same length.
Tapers trade beamwidth for sidelobes: for five elements, uniform −12 dB at 20.8°, Chebyshev −20 dB at 23.7°, binomial none at 30.3°.
A phase step α = −βd cosθ₀ steers the beam; fixed phase shifters make it squint with frequency.
A Yagi gets its phases from rod lengths and spacings and is narrowband; an LPDA scales its geometry by τ and stays wideband as its active region slides.
Horns and dishes are apertures: G = 4πA<sub>e</sub>/λ²; a dish gives η(πD/λ)², 39.8 dBi and 1.75° for 3 m at 4 GHz.
A patch is about half a guided wavelength long, radiates from two in-phase edges and needs an inset or probe to reach 50 Ω.
Measure in the far field (R ≥ 2D²/λ): gain by substitution or the two- and three-antenna methods, pattern by rotation, polarization by a spinning probe.
Ground waves serve LF and MF, sky waves HF (f<sub>c</sub> = 9√N, MUF = f<sub>c</sub> sec φ), and space waves VHF and above up to the radio horizon.
bank_note: Long answers in most syllabi ask for the array factor with broadside and end-fire conditions, a Dolph-Chebyshev or binomial design worked to currents, Yagi and log-periodic design relations, horn, dish and patch dimensions from given gain or frequency, the gain-measurement methods, and MUF and skip-distance numericals. Several questions below join two or more chapters.

bank.q: State the principle of pattern multiplication. Derive the array factor of two identical isotropic sources spaced d apart with a feed phase difference α, and use it to find the maxima and nulls for d = λ/2 with (a) α = 0 and (b) α = π.
outline: Two sources on the z axis, path difference d cosθ, ψ = βd cosθ + α
Maxima at ψ = 2mπ, nulls at ψ = (2m + 1)π inside the visible range
Broadside and end-fire pairs with a table of values
Pattern multiplication: element pattern × array factor, union of nulls
answer: Set-up. Element 1 sits at the origin and element 2 at z = d. Their currents are I and I ejα. The direction θ is measured from the +z axis (the array axis), and β = 2π/λ.

Phase difference. A far point in direction θ is closer to element 2 by d cosθ, so wave 2 arrives ahead in phase by βd cosθ. Adding the feed lead α, the total phase of wave 2 relative to wave 1 is ψ = βd cosθ + α.

answer.text: Array factor. With equal amplitudes and the far-field distance factor taken out:
answer.pre:
AF = 1 + e<sup>jψ</sup> = e<sup>jψ/2</sup>(e<sup>−jψ/2</sup> + e<sup>jψ/2</sup>) = 2 e<sup>jψ/2</sup> cos(ψ/2)
|AF| = 2|cos(ψ/2)|,  normalized |AF<sub>n</sub>| = |cos(ψ/2)|

answer: Maxima and nulls. |AF| = 2 when ψ = 0, ±2π, …; AF = 0 when ψ = ±π, ±3π, …. As θ goes from 0° to 180°, ψ sweeps from βd + α to −βd + α, so only these values count. For d = λ/2, βd = π.
(a) α = 0. ψ = π cosθ, visible range −π to π. Maximum ψ = 0 at cosθ = 0, θ = 90° (broadside). Nulls ψ = ±π at cosθ = ±1, θ = 0° and 180°.
(b) α = π. ψ = π cosθ + π, visible range 0 to 2π. Maxima ψ = 0 and 2π at cosθ = −1 and +1: θ = 180° and 0°, both ends of the axis (end-fire both ways). Null ψ = π at cosθ = 0, θ = 90°.

Pattern multiplication. For identical elements with the same orientation, element 2 radiates the same field shape as element 1, shifted in phase by ψ. So the total field is E = Ee(θ, φ) × AF(θ, φ): the element pattern times the array factor, and the power pattern is |Ee|²|AF|². Every null of the element and every null of the array factor is a null of the total.

Example of the product. Two half-wave dipoles parallel to x, spaced λ/2 along z and fed in phase: in the x-z plane the element has nulls along ±x and the array factor (case a) has nulls along ±z, so the total pattern has four nulls and four lobes between them.
Limits. The rule needs identical, identically oriented elements; strong mutual coupling makes the currents unequal and the product then holds only approximately.
Check. At θ = 60° with α = 0: ψ = π/2 and |cos(π/4)| = 0.707; with α = π: ψ = 3π/2 and |cos(3π/4)| = 0.707. Both rows of the table agree, and each row has its maximum where ψ = 0 or 2π.

bank.q: Derive the normalized array factor of an N-element uniform linear array. Give the conditions for broadside and ordinary end-fire operation, the null and grating-lobe conditions, and work them out for N = 4 with d = λ/2 (broadside) and d = λ/4 (end-fire).
outline: Main beam ψ = 0; broadside α = 0; end-fire α = −βd
Nulls ψ = ±2πm/N; grating lobes at ψ = ±2π
answer: Set-up. N equal elements on the z axis, spacing d, element n fed with I ejnα. The wave from element n reaches a far point in direction θ ahead by nβd cosθ, so neighbours differ by the same ψ = βd cosθ + α.

answer.text: Sum. The array factor is a geometric series with ratio ejψ:
answer.pre:
AF = 1 + e<sup>jψ</sup> + … + e<sup>j(N−1)ψ</sup> = (e<sup>jNψ</sup> − 1)/(e<sup>jψ</sup> − 1)
   = e<sup>j(N−1)ψ/2</sup> · sin(Nψ/2)/sin(ψ/2)
|AF<sub>n</sub>| = |sin(Nψ/2) / (N sin(ψ/2))|

answer: Main beam. As ψ → 0 the ratio tends to N, so the normalized maximum 1 is at ψ = 0.
Broadside. The beam at θ = 90° needs ψ = 0 there: βd cos 90° + α = 0, so α = 0.
Ordinary end-fire. The beam at θ = 0° needs βd + α = 0, so α = −βd; α = +βd puts it at 180°.
Nulls. sin(Nψ/2) = 0 with sin(ψ/2) ≠ 0: ψ = ±2πm/N, m = 1, 2, … but not a multiple of N.

Grating lobes. At ψ = ±2π the ratio is N again: a second full beam. It appears if ±2π lies in the visible range βd + α to −βd + α. Broadside (range ±βd) needs d ≥ λ; end-fire (range 0 to −2βd) needs only d ≥ λ/2.

N = 4, d = λ/2, broadside. ψ = π cosθ. Nulls ψ = ±π/2 and ±π: cosθ = ±0.5 and ±1, so θ = 60°, 120°, 0° and 180°. FNBW = 60°. Half power at ψ = ±0.715 rad gives θ = 76.8° and 103.2°, HPBW = 26.3°. First sidelobe 0.272 (−11.3 dB) at 42.9°. No grating lobe since d < λ.

N = 4, d = λ/4, end-fire. α = −π/2, ψ = (π/2)(cosθ − 1), range 0 to −π. Nulls ψ = −π/2 and −π: cosθ = 0 and −1, θ = 90° and 180°. Half power at θ = 57.0°, so the full HPBW across the axis is 114°. Grating lobe would need ψ = −2π, outside the range.
Sketch. Broadside: a disc-shaped beam round the axis peaking at 90°, small lobes near 43° and 137°. End-fire: one wide lobe along +z, nothing toward −z.
Check. At θ = 30° broadside, ψ = π × 0.866 = 2.721 rad; sin(5.441)/(4 sin(1.360)) = −0.745/(4 × 0.978) = −0.190, magnitude 0.19 as in the table.

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of the Yagi-Uda antenna and the log-periodic dipole array. Define the active region, explain why the LPDA is wideband, and give the design relations with an example.
outline: Yagi: driven element, reflector, directors, typical lengths and spacings
Why the beam goes toward the directors; narrow band
LPDA: τ, σ, apex angle, crossed feed, active region
answer: Yagi-Uda construction. A boom carries one driven half-wave (often folded) dipole of 0.46λ to 0.48λ, one reflector of 0.50λ to 0.55λ placed 0.15λ to 0.25λ behind it, and directors of 0.40λ to 0.45λ, 0.15λ to 0.35λ apart, in front. Only the driven element is connected to the feeder.

How it works. The driven element’s field induces currents in the parasitic rods. A rod longer than resonance is inductive, a shorter rod capacitive, so length sets the phase of the induced current; spacing adds a path phase. The reflector then acts like the rear element of a cardioid pair and cancels radiation toward the back, while the directors stay in step with the forward-moving wave: the Yagi is an end-fire array firing toward the directors.

Yagi numbers. At 500 MHz (λ = 600 mm): reflector 300 mm, driven element 282 mm, director 270 mm, spacings 150 mm and 120 mm, gain about 7 dBi. Gain rises with more directors (9 to 11 dBi for five elements), but the phases are right only near the design frequency, so the band is 2 to 5 %.

LPDA construction. Dipoles shrink by the scale factor τ = Ln+1/Ln from back to front; the spacing factor is σ = dn/(2Ln); the dipole tips lie on lines from an apex at half angle α = tan⁻¹[(1 − τ)/(4σ)]. All dipoles hang on a two-wire line with crossed connections, fed at the short end.

Active region. At any frequency only the dipoles near λ/2 carry large current; these few form the active region. Longer dipoles behind it are inductive and weak, shorter ones in front are too small. The crossed feed makes the active dipoles fire toward the short end: with d ≈ 0.15λ (βd = 54°), the waves of neighbours cancel toward the back (180° apart) and arrive 288° (that is −72°) apart toward the front, so they add.

Why wideband. The geometry repeats when the frequency is multiplied by 1/τ, and the active region simply slides along the boom. Between fmin (longest dipole active) and fmax (shortest active), impedance and pattern stay nearly constant.

answer.pre:
B = f<sub>max</sub>/f<sub>min</sub>,   N = 1 + ln B / ln(1/τ)
L<sub>1</sub> = λ<sub>max</sub>/2,   L<sub>N</sub> = L<sub>1</sub> τ<sup>N−1</sup>,   d<sub>n</sub> = 2σL<sub>n</sub>
boom = (L<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>N</sub>)/(2 tan α)

answer: Check. The shortest dipole is λ/2 at 150/0.2354 = 637 MHz, above fmax, and the 11 spacings 225 + 202.5 + … + 78.5 add to 1544 mm, the boom length found from the apex angle.

bank.q: Explain how a horn antenna radiates and why its flare must be chosen with care. State Babinet’s principle as extended by Booker and show how the impedance of a slot follows from that of its complementary dipole.
outline: E-plane, H-plane, pyramidal, conical and corrugated horns
Phase error δ = a²/(8ℓ) and the optimum horn
Babinet and Booker: complementary screens, E and H swapped
answer: Aperture radiation. A horn is a flared waveguide. The TE10 field grows with the flare to fill a large opening, and this aperture field radiates. Its gain follows G = 4πAe/λ², with Ae = ηapA; the flare also lowers the reflection that an open waveguide end would cause.

Types. E-plane sectoral (narrow walls flared), H-plane sectoral (broad walls flared), pyramidal (both, the usual gain standard), conical (circular guide) and corrugated (ringed walls, symmetric pattern, low cross-polarization).

Phase error. The wave inside the flare spreads from the apex, so it reaches the edge of an opening of width a a distance δ ≈ a²/(8ℓ) behind the centre, where ℓ is the apex length. A wide, short horn has a large δ: the nulls fill, the sidelobes rise and the gain drops.
Optimum horn. For a given length the gain peaks at δ = 0.25λ in the E-plane and 0.375λ in the H-plane, giving ℓE = B²/(2λ), ℓH = A²/(3λ), ηap ≈ 0.5, HPBWE ≈ 56λ/B and HPBWH ≈ 67λ/A degrees.

answer.text: Example (10 GHz, λ = 3 cm, A = 10 cm, B = 8 cm, ηap = 0.5):

answer: Babinet and Booker. Babinet: the fields behind a screen with an opening and behind its complementary screen add to the unscreened field. Booker: for electromagnetic waves the complementary screen must also have E and H interchanged, so the sum is a vector sum with the polarization turned 90°.
Slot from dipole. A narrow slot in a large conducting sheet therefore has the pattern of the complementary strip dipole with E and H swapped: a horizontal slot radiates like a vertical dipole.

answer.pre:
Z<sub>slot</sub> Z<sub>dipole</sub> = η<sub>0</sub>²/4 = (120π)²/4 = 35 530 Ω²
Z<sub>dipole</sub> = 73 + j42.5 Ω  →  Z<sub>slot</sub> = 35 530 (73 − j42.5)/7135 = 363 − j212 Ω
resonant dipole 73 Ω  →  Z<sub>slot</sub> = 487 Ω

answer: Consequences. The slot is a high-impedance antenna, and an inductive dipole gives a capacitive slot. Slots are flush with the surface, so they suit aircraft skins and slotted-waveguide radar arrays.

bank.q: Explain ground-wave, sky-wave and space-wave propagation. Describe the layers of the ionosphere and define critical frequency, maximum usable frequency and skip distance. Find f<sub>c</sub>, the MUF for 1000 km and the skip distance at 15 MHz for an F2 layer with N<sub>max</sub> = 1.24 × 10¹² m⁻³ at 300 km.
outline: D, E, F1, F2 layers and day/night changes
Secant law, flat-earth MUF and skip distance
answer: Ground wave. LF and MF (about 30 kHz to 3 MHz). The wave follows the earth’s surface; it needs vertical polarization and loses more over dry ground than over sea. Used by AM medium wave and maritime radio.
Sky wave. HF (3 to 30 MHz). The ionosphere refracts the wave back to earth, giving one or more hops over thousands of kilometres. Used by shortwave broadcasting and long-distance HF.
Space wave. VHF and above. Direct and ground-reflected rays between antennas in line of sight; range set by antenna heights, d ≈ 4.12(√ht + √hr) km.

Layers. D (60 to 90 km, daytime, absorbs MF and low HF); E (90 to 150 km, daytime refraction, sporadic E); F1 (150 to 250 km, daytime) and F2 (250 to 400 km, highest density, main HF reflector; F1 and F2 merge at night).
Why it bends. The plasma index is n = √(1 − 81N/f²). As a wave climbs into rising N, n falls and the ray bends away from the vertical until it turns back.
Critical frequency. The highest frequency returned at vertical incidence: n = 0 at Nmax gives fc = 9√Nmax.

MUF. At oblique incidence a higher frequency still returns: MUF = fc sec φ, φ being the ray angle from the vertical. Over a flat earth with the layer at height h and stations D apart, MUF = fc√(1 + (D/2h)²).
Skip distance. The shortest ground distance at which a frequency f > fc returns: Dskip = 2h√((f/fc)² − 1). The skip zone lies between the end of the ground wave and Dskip.
Sketch. Earth line, F2 layer at 300 km, ray up at 59° from the vertical landing at 1000 km; a steeper ray at 15 MHz landing at 668 km; the skip zone shaded between the ground-wave range and 668 km.
Check. At 15 MHz the 1000 km path needs 15 < 19.5 MHz, so it works, and 1000 km lies beyond the 668 km skip distance, as it must.

bank.q: Ten isotropic elements are spaced λ/4 apart. Find, for broadside, ordinary end-fire and Hansen-Woodyard end-fire phasing, the progressive phase, the first-null beamwidth, the half-power beamwidth and the directivity, and comment on the results.
answer: Data. N = 10, d = λ/4, so βd = π/2 (90°) and the array length is Nd = 2.5λ. θ is measured from the array axis.
Broadside phase. α = 0, ψ = (π/2)cosθ.
Broadside FNBW. First nulls at ψ = ±2π/10: (π/2)cosθ = ±π/5, cosθ = ±0.4, θ = 66.4° and 113.6°. FNBW = 47.2°, the same as 2 sin⁻¹(λ/(Nd)) = 2 sin⁻¹0.4.
Broadside HPBW and D. HPBW ≈ 50.8/(Nd/λ) = 50.8/2.5 = 20.3° (the exact pattern gives 20.5°). D ≈ 2Nd/λ = 5.0, that is 7.0 dBi (numerical integration gives 5.17).
End-fire phase. α = −βd = −90° per element, so ψ = (π/2)(cosθ − 1) and the beam is along +z.
End-fire FNBW. First null at ψ = −2π/10: cosθ − 1 = −0.4, cosθ = 0.6, θ = 53.1°. FNBW = 2 × 53.1° = 106.3° = 2 cos⁻¹(1 − λ/(Nd)).
End-fire HPBW and D. HPBW ≈ 2 cos⁻¹(1 − 0.443/2.5) = 2 cos⁻¹0.8228 = 69.3° (exact 69.4°). D ≈ 4Nd/λ = 10, that is 10.0 dBi.

Hansen-Woodyard. α = −(βd + π/N) = −(90° + 18°) = −108° per element. The extra phase puts the peak at ψ = −π/10, where the normalized sum is only 0.639 of the in-phase value, but narrows the beam: HPBW about 38.6°, first null at 36.9°, and D ≈ 17.8 (12.5 dBi) by numerical integration, 1.78 times the ordinary end-fire value.

Comment. The broadside beam is narrow in θ but is a disc all round the axis; the end-fire beam is wider in θ but is a single pencil, so its directivity is double. Hansen-Woodyard trades a higher sidelobe and a tighter phase tolerance for about 2.5 dB more directivity.
Grating-lobe check. Broadside needs d < λ and end-fire d < λ/2; d = λ/4 satisfies both, and for Hansen-Woodyard ψ reaches only −(π + π/10) at θ = 180°, short of −2π.

Where the beamwidth formulas come from. For broadside, setting Nψ/2 = ±π with ψ = βd cosθ gives cosθ = ±λ/(Nd), and the angle from broadside is sin⁻¹(λ/Nd). For end-fire, ψ = βd(cosθ − 1) = −2π/N gives 1 − cosθ = λ/(Nd), so the null angle from the axis is cos⁻¹(1 − λ/Nd); near the axis cosθ changes slowly, which is why the end-fire beam is wider.
Check. 2 × 2.5 = 5 and 4 × 2.5 = 10, as the long-array formulas give; the integrated values 5.17 and 10.0 agree within 4 %.

bank.q: Design a 5-element broadside Dolph-Chebyshev array with d = λ/2 and a sidelobe level of −20 dB. Find the excitation currents and the first nulls, and compare the design with uniform and binomial arrays of five elements.
outline: R from the sidelobe level, x₀ = cosh[cosh⁻¹R/(N − 1)]
Array factor as a cosine series in u = ψ/2
answer: Step 1: R. SLL = 20 dB below the peak, so R = 1020/20 = 10.

answer.text: Step 3: array factor. Number the elements −2 … 2 about the centre, currents I2, I1, I0, I1, I2, u = ψ/2 = (π/2)cosθ:
answer.pre:
AF = I<sub>0</sub> + 2I<sub>1</sub> cos 2u + 2I<sub>2</sub> cos 4u
cos 2u = 2cos²u − 1,   cos 4u = 8cos⁴u − 8cos²u + 1
AF = 16I<sub>2</sub> cos⁴u + (4I<sub>1</sub> − 16I<sub>2</sub>) cos²u + (I<sub>0</sub> − 2I<sub>1</sub> + 2I<sub>2</sub>)

answer.text: Step 4: match T₄. With x = x0 cos u, T4(x) = 8x0⁴cos⁴u − 8x0²cos²u + 1:

answer: Step 5: normalize. Dividing by the edge current: 1 : 1.609 : 1.932 : 1.609 : 1. Dividing by the centre instead: 0.518 : 0.833 : 1 : 0.833 : 0.518.
Step 6: peak check. At u = 0, AF = 2.7024 + 2(2.2500) + 2(1.3988) = 10.000 = R, as T4(x0) = R requires.

Step 7: nulls. T4(x) = cos(4 cos⁻¹x) = 0 first at x = cos(π/8) = 0.9239. cos u = 0.9239/1.2933 = 0.7144, u = 0.775 rad, ψ = 1.550 rad, cosθ = ψ/π = 0.4934, θ = 60.4° and 119.6°. FNBW = 59.1°. The second nulls at x = cos(3π/8) = 0.3827 give cos u = 0.2959, ψ = 2.541 rad, θ = 36.0° and 144.0°.

Step 8: sidelobes. Between the nulls T4 swings to ±1, so every sidelobe is 1/10 of the peak, −20 dB, including the lobes at the ends of the axis (θ = 0° and 180°, where x = x0 cos(π/2) = 0 and T4(0) = 1).

Step 10: discussion. Lowering the sidelobes always widens the beam and lowers the directivity. The Chebyshev design pays only 2.9° of beamwidth and 0.28 dB of directivity for 8 dB lower sidelobes; the binomial design removes them but pays 9.5° and 1.36 dB, and its edge currents are 1/6 of the centre current.

Step 11: why Chebyshev is optimum. Tm(x) rises faster beyond x = 1 than any other polynomial of the same degree that stays within ±1 on [−1, 1], so for a given sidelobe ratio R it reaches R at the smallest x0, which means the narrowest main beam.

bank.q: A 12 GHz satellite ground terminal needs at least 40 dBi with an aperture efficiency of 0.6. Find the smallest dish diameter, then choose a 1.2 m dish with f/D = 0.35 and find its gain, half-power and first-null beamwidths, focal length, depth, feed angle and the far-field distance for measuring it.
outline: λ and G = η(πD/λ)² solved for D
Gain of the chosen 1.2 m dish
R ≥ 2D²/λ and comments on feed and surface
answer: Smallest diameter. 40 dBi is G = 10⁴. From G = η(πD/λ)²: πD/λ = √(10⁴/0.6) = 129.1, so D = 129.1 × 0.025/π = 1.03 m.
Chosen dish. D = 1.2 m gives D/λ = 48, πD/λ = 150.8, (πD/λ)² = 22 740 and G = 0.6 × 22 740 = 13 644, that is 41.3 dBi, a 1.3 dB margin over the requirement.
Beamwidths. HPBW ≈ 70λ/D = 70/48 = 1.46°; BWFN ≈ 140/48 = 2.92°. The terminal must point within about ±0.3° to keep the pointing loss small (half the HPBW costs 3 dB).
Feed angle. tan(ψ0/2) = D/(4f) = 1.2/1.68 = 0.7143, ψ0/2 = 35.5°, ψ0 = 71.1°. The feed horn must cover ±71° with its edge about 10 dB down, a wide-beam feed; a deeper dish needs a still wider feed.
Measurement distance. R ≥ 2D²/λ = 2 × 1.44/0.025 = 115 m, too long for most chambers, so such a dish is measured on an outdoor range, a compact range or a near-field scanner.
Surface tolerance. To lose under about 0.8 dB by Ruze’s rule, the RMS surface error should be near λ/30 = 0.8 mm; λ/16 = 1.6 mm would cost 2.7 dB and wipe out the margin.
Feed choice. A prime-focus feed suits a 1.2 m dish; an offset geometry would avoid blockage and is the usual choice for such terminals.

Illumination. The feed should light the rim about 10 dB below the centre: brighter, and spillover past the rim wastes power and lets in warm ground noise; dimmer, and the outer dish is wasted. With η = 0.6 assumed, this balance, blockage and surface error must together cost no more than 2.2 dB below a uniformly lit aperture.
Check. 4πAe/λ² with Ae = 0.6 × π × 0.36 = 0.6786 m²: 4π × 0.6786/0.000625 = 13 644, the same gain.

bank.q: Design a rectangular microstrip patch for 5.8 GHz on a substrate with ε<sub>r</sub> = 2.2 and h = 1.575 mm using the transmission-line model. Find W, ε<sub>eff</sub>, ΔL and L, estimate the edge resistance and the inset depth for a 50 Ω feed, and sketch the patch.
outline: L = λ<sub>g</sub>/2 − 2ΔL and a frequency check
answer: Free-space values. λ0 = 3 × 10⁸/5.8 × 10⁹ = 51.72 mm; c/(2f) = 25.86 mm.
Frequency check. f = c/[2(L + 2ΔL)√εeff] = 3 × 10⁸/(2 × 0.01814 × 1.4257) = 5.80 GHz.
Edge resistance. G1 ≈ W/(120λ0) = 20.45/(120 × 51.72) = 3.294 × 10⁻³ S, so Redge ≈ 1/(2G1) = 152 Ω (slot coupling makes the true value somewhat lower).

Sketch. A 16.5 mm (L) by 20.4 mm (W) rectangle over a ground plane, the two edges W long marked as radiating slots, a 50 Ω line entering one radiating edge through a 5.0 mm notch. Mode TM10, linear polarization along L, beam broadside to the board.

Remarks. The low εr gives a larger, more efficient patch with a wider band than FR-4 (about 3 to 4 % here). The patch is 0.32λ0 long and 0.40λ0 wide, so four of them fit at λ0/2 = 25.9 mm spacing in an array.

Why these steps. The width formula gives a patch wide enough to radiate efficiently without exciting higher-order modes; εeff then depends on W/h, and ΔL on both, so the order W → εeff → ΔL → L cannot be changed. If the board thickness or εr changes, all four must be recomputed.

Feed alternatives. A coaxial probe placed 5.0 mm in from the radiating edge on the centre line would also see about 50 Ω and avoids the notch; on this 1.575 mm board its series inductance is small. An aperture-coupled feed would need a second board.
Check. L/λg = 16.50/36.28 = 0.455, just under 0.5 because of the 2ΔL correction, as expected.

bank.q: Describe the far-field condition and the substitution, two-antenna and three-antenna methods of gain measurement, with pattern and polarization measurement. Work the numbers for a 10 GHz range: test antenna 0.3 m across, standard horn 15 dBi, readings −30 and −25 dBm; two identical horns 6 m apart giving −30 dBm for 0 dBm transmitted.
outline: Pattern cuts and polarization, axial ratio
answer: Far field. The source wave must be nearly plane over the test aperture. Limiting the extra path at the aperture edge to λ/16 gives R ≥ 2D²/λ, with R between phase centres and D the largest dimension. Here λ = 0.03 m and R ≥ 2 × 0.09/0.03 = 6 m.

Range. Use an anechoic chamber or an elevated outdoor range; keep reflections out (absorber, clear path, time gating) and keep cables and connectors identical between readings, on both transmit and receive sides.
Substitution. A fixed source transmits; the receiver reads Pstd with the standard horn, then Ptest with the test antenna in the same place: Gtest = Gstd + (Ptest − Pstd) = 15 + (−25 + 30) = 20 dBi.

answer.text: Two-antenna method. Friis in dB for identical antennas:

answer: Three-antenna method. Three different antennas measured in pairs give G1 + G2, G1 + G3 and G2 + G3. With sums 38.0, 35.0 and 33.0 dB, the total is 53.0 dB and G1 = 20.0, G2 = 18.0, G3 = 15.0 dBi. No standard is needed, only R, λ and accurate power readings.

Pattern. Turn the test antenna about its phase centre on a positioner and record received power; cut in the E-plane (containing E and the beam axis) and the H-plane; normalize to the peak and read HPBW, nulls and sidelobes. Rotating the source 90° gives the cross-polar pattern.

Polarization. Spin a linear probe: a deep minimum means linear, a constant level circular, a swing between Emax and Emin elliptical, with axial ratio AR = Emax/Emin. A 6 dB power swing means AR = 106/20 = 2. Two crossed probes with phase give the sense; confirm with known right-hand and left-hand circular horns.
Check. 20.0 + 18.0 = 38.0, 20.0 + 15.0 = 35.0, 18.0 + 15.0 = 33.0: all three pair sums are reproduced.

bank.q: Four of the 5.8 GHz patches of the patch-design question form a linear phased array that must scan ±30° from broadside without grating lobes, with room to reach 45°. Choose the spacing, find the phase settings for 0°, 15° and 30°, the beamwidth at broadside and at 30°, the beam squint at 5.7 and 5.9 GHz, and estimate the array gain.
outline: Spacing and fit of the 20.4 mm patch
α = −βd sinθ<sub>s</sub> from broadside and element phases
HPBW at broadside and steered, squint with fixed phase shifters
Gain estimate by pattern multiplication and comments
answer: Wavelength. λ0 = 51.72 mm at 5.8 GHz. Scan angles here are measured from broadside, θs = 90° − θ0, so the step is α = −βd sinθs.
Spacing limit. No grating lobe needs d/λ < 1/(1 + sinθs): 0.667 (34.5 mm) at 30°, 0.586 (30.3 mm) at 45°.
Choice. d = λ0/2 = 25.9 mm meets both limits with margin. The patches are 20.45 mm wide, leaving a 5.4 mm gap for the feed lines; mutual coupling at this spacing is moderate.
Beamwidth at broadside. The 4-element factor with d = λ/2 has HPBW = 26.3° (half-power points at ψ = ±0.715 rad).
Beamwidth at 30°. Computed from the array factor, the steered beam has HPBW = 30.9°. It broadens roughly as 1/cosθs (26.3/0.866 = 30.4°) because the array looks shorter from an oblique direction.

Squint. With fixed phase shifters the steering sine scales as f0/f: at 5.7 GHz sinθs = 0.5 × 5.8/5.7 = 0.5088, θs = 30.6°; at 5.9 GHz 0.4915, θs = 29.4°. A ±0.6° wander is small against the 31° beam, so phase shifters are adequate across this band.

Pattern multiplication. The total pattern is the patch pattern (broad, about cos θs-shaped in the scan plane, near 7 dBi at broadside) times the array factor. Toward 30° the element itself is down about 1.2 dB, so the scanned beam loses gain beyond the array-factor effect.

Gain estimate. Four equal elements add about 10 log 4 = 6.0 dB: 7 + 6 = 13 dBi at broadside, less the loss of the printed feed network (about 0.5 to 1 dB at 5.8 GHz), so roughly 12 dBi. At 30° about 1.2 dB less from the element pattern.
Coupling. At λ/2 spacing the patches load one another, so each element’s input impedance changes with the scan angle; the feed is matched at broadside and checked again at ±30°.

Optional taper. If the −11.3 dB sidelobes of the uniform four are too high, a binomial-like 1 : 2 : 2 : 1 or a Chebyshev taper lowers them at the cost of a wider beam, as in the five-element comparison.
Check. At θs = 30°, ψ = 180° × sin30° − 90° = 0, so the four waves add in phase in the wanted direction; the grating lobe would need ψ = −360°, which needs sinθs = −1.5, impossible.

bank.q: Choose and justify an antenna for each job, and say how far apart the antennas must be when each is measured: (a) surveying TV signals from 470 to 860 MHz, (b) a 40 km point-to-point microwave link at 6 GHz needing about 39 dBi, (c) a gain standard for a 10 GHz lab, (d) a fixed 500 MHz telemetry receiver pointing at one transmitter.
outline: LPDA for the survey, with τ and N
Dish for the link, with D, HPBW
Pyramidal horn as standard, Yagi for telemetry
Far-field distances and a summary table
answer: (a) TV survey, 470 to 860 MHz. The band ratio is 860/470 = 1.83, far beyond a Yagi’s 2 to 5 %. An LPDA keeps its pattern across it. With τ = 0.9: N = 1 + ln 1.83/ln(1/0.9) = 1 + 0.604/0.1054 = 6.7, so 7 dipoles (designers add one or two more to cover the end effects). L1 = 150/470 = 0.319 m. Gain 6 to 8 dBi, flat across the band.

(b) 6 GHz link needing 39 dBi. Only a reflector gives this gain at a sensible size. With η = 0.55: πD/λ = √(103.9/0.55) = 120.2 and λ = 0.05 m, so D = 1.91 m; a 2 m dish gives 0.55(π × 40)² = 8685 = 39.4 dBi and HPBW ≈ 70/40 = 1.75°, which also keeps interference from other links low.

(c) 10 GHz gain standard. A pyramidal horn: its gain follows from its dimensions to a few tenths of a dB, it has no resonant parts, and it is broadband. A 10 cm × 8 cm optimum horn gives about 17.5 dBi with near-equal E- and H-plane beams (21.0° and 20.1°).

(d) 500 MHz telemetry, fixed direction. A narrow band and one direction suit a Yagi: a 3-element design (reflector 300 mm, driven 282 mm, director 270 mm on a 270 mm boom) gives about 7 dBi; five or six elements reach 10 dBi at low cost and weight.

Far-field distances. R ≥ 2D²/λ with D the largest dimension: LPDA at 860 MHz, D ≈ 0.32 m, λ = 0.349 m → 0.59 m, but R must also be several λ, so about 3 m. 2 m dish at 6 GHz: 2 × 4/0.05 = 160 m. Horn at 10 GHz, D = 0.1 m: 0.67 m, so a 2 to 3 m chamber range is ample. Yagi at 500 MHz, largest dimension the 0.30 m reflector: 0.3 m, again set by the several-λ rule to about 3 m.

Trade-offs. Gain rises with electrical size: the dish is 40λ across, the horn 3.3λ, the Yagi and LPDA under a wavelength across but longer along the boom. Bandwidth goes the other way for resonant designs: the Yagi is narrow, the LPDA and horn broad, and the dish as broad as its feed.

Measuring the dish. 160 m is too long indoors, so the dish is measured on an outdoor range with both antennas on towers, or on a compact range or near-field scanner; substitution against a standard horn still gives its gain.
Check. 0.55 × (π × 2/0.05)² = 0.55 × 15 791 = 8685, and 10 log 8685 = 39.4 dBi, which meets the 39 dBi target.

bank.q: An HF link must work over 1500 km. By day the F2 layer has f<sub>c</sub> = 10 MHz at a virtual height of 300 km; at night f<sub>c</sub> = 4 MHz at 350 km. Find the MUF and the optimum working frequency for day and night, check the skip distance, and explain why one frequency cannot serve all day. Compare with a VHF line-of-sight link from a 50 m tower to a 10 m mast.
outline: Day and night values, OWF = 0.85 MUF
D-layer absorption and night fall of f<sub>c</sub>
answer: Method. For stations D apart and a layer at h, the ray meets the layer at φ with tanφ = (D/2)/h, so sec φ = √(1 + (D/2h)²) and MUF = fc sec φ. The optimum working frequency is taken as 0.85 × MUF.

Skip check. Dskip = 2h√((f/fc)² − 1). Day at 22.9 MHz: 600 × √(2.289² − 1) = 600 × 2.059 = 1235 km. Night at 8.0 MHz: 700 × √(2.010² − 1) = 700 × 1.744 = 1221 km. Both are under 1500 km, so the receiver lies beyond the skip zone.

Why the frequency must change. At night 22.9 MHz is far above the 9.46 MHz MUF and passes through the layer. By day 8 MHz is below the MUF, but the D layer absorbs low HF strongly by day and the skip zone shrinks; the signal is weak. So stations keep a day frequency and a night frequency and change near dawn and dusk.

Single hop. φ near 65° to 68° means a low take-off angle, so the antenna should radiate well a few degrees to about 20° above the horizon; a flat-earth model is fair at 1500 km, but beyond about 4000 km earth curvature forces two hops.

VHF comparison. d ≈ 4.12(√50 + √10) = 4.12 × (7.07 + 3.16) = 42.2 km. A VHF link is steady and wideband but needs relays every few tens of kilometres; HF reaches 1500 km in one hop with no infrastructure but changes with the sun and season.

Lower limit and fading. The lowest usable frequency is set by D-layer absorption and noise rather than by the layer geometry, so by day it may sit near 8 to 10 MHz on this path, which again rules out the night frequency. Even at the right frequency, rays by slightly different paths interfere and the signal fades by 10 to 20 dB over seconds, so HF links use diversity or robust modulation.
Check. For the day path, cos φ = 300/√(300² + 750²) = 300/807.8 = 0.3714 and 1/0.3714 = 2.693, the same secant.

glossary.def: The few log-periodic dipoles near half a wavelength long that carry most of the current at a given frequency.
The ratio of effective aperture to physical aperture area; it counts amplitude taper, phase error, spillover and blockage.
The pattern of an array of isotropic elements; multiplied by the element pattern it gives the array pattern.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest field in one turn of the polarization ellipse; 1 (0 dB) for circular.
The movement of a phased-array beam with frequency when the steering uses fixed phase shifts.
An array whose currents follow Pascal’s triangle; it has no sidelobes when d ≤ λ/2.
Z<sub>slot</sub>Z<sub>dipole</sub> = η₀²/4, linking a slot’s impedance to that of its complementary dipole.
An array whose beam is perpendicular to its axis, obtained with equal phases.
A reflector feed that uses a hyperbolic subreflector inside the focus to place the feed behind the dish.
The highest frequency an ionospheric layer returns at vertical incidence, f<sub>c</sub> = 9√N<sub>max</sub>.
An array whose currents make every sidelobe equal to a chosen level and the beam as narrow as possible for it.
An array whose beam lies along its axis, obtained with a phase step α = −βd.
The distance 2D²/λ beyond which the measured pattern no longer depends on distance.
A second full-size beam that appears when the element spacing is too large for the scan angle.
An end-fire array with an extra phase π/N per element, giving about 1.8 times the directivity.
A wideband array of dipoles whose lengths and spacings scale by a fixed ratio τ.
The highest frequency that returns over a given oblique sky-wave path, f<sub>c</sub> sec φ.
A horn whose flare gives the most gain for its length, with edge phase error 0.25λ (E-plane) and 0.375λ (H-plane).
A Yagi rod not connected to the feed, driven by the field of the driven element.
The rule that an array of identical, identically oriented elements has the element pattern times the array factor.
An array whose beam is steered electronically by setting the phase of each element.
The line-of-sight range with standard refraction, 4.12√h km for h in metres.
The shortest ground distance at which a sky wave of a given frequency returns.
The region between the end of the ground wave and the skip distance where no signal is received.
Feed power that misses a reflector, wasting power and adding ground noise on receive.
The values of ψ that real directions produce, from βd + α down to −βd + α.
